overview: This broad atlas label covers varied Anatolian communities between about 2000 and 1500 BCE, including cities with palaces, workshops and trade connections. It is not the name of one tribe, language or empire. The outline includes Beycesultan and Acemhöyük but excludes Kanesh and Hattusha; evidence from those neighboring cities must be identified separately. Hittite, Luwian, Phrygian and Lydian histories are not interchangeable.

periods.title: Cities and palatial centers
periods.summary: Middle Bronze Age towns developed substantial public buildings and long-distance connections; Beycesultan provides one western example.

periods.title: Changing households and regional powers
periods.summary: Beycesultan layers dated about 1700-1595 and 1600-1500 BCE preserve rebuilding and intensive household textile work.

items.text: Beycesultan in the upper Meander valley was far more than a scattering of tents. Its Middle Bronze Age remains include the substantial building conventionally called the Burnt Palace and other public structures. The original excavators investigated possible connections with Arzawa, but a palace does not supply its ruler’s name. The ancient identity of the city remains uncertain.

The British Institute’s excavations at Beycesultan ran for six seasons between 1954 and 1959. Field notes, plans, photographs and drawings preserve how the city was uncovered. These records matter because later researchers can compare buildings and finds with their original excavation contexts instead of treating attractive objects as isolated treasures.

Acemhöyük linked an urban center with people who raised animals beyond its streets. An animal-bone study argues that mobile herders supplied animal products while specialized processing and distribution took place in the town. It also suggests that wool producers responded to wider markets and often operated beyond close central control. A powerful palace did not necessarily direct every flock.

At Beycesultan, a building dated about 1915-1745 BCE contained a courtyard hearth, storage jars and clay basins. A burnt textile lay near grain and the remains of baskets made from branches. These finds bring food storage and cloth work into the same excavated setting, although the limited exposure leaves the building’s full layout uncertain.

That early textile, called Tx1, held a colorful surprise: chemical analysis detected evidence of an indigo dye. Its fibres resemble hemp, and its looped structure suggests a technique known as nålbinding, made with a needle rather than a loom. The researchers propose locally available woad as a likely dye source. The specific plant and technique remain interpretations.

In another Beycesultan house, room 28, dated about 1700-1595 BCE, had clay storage chests, cooking pots and a large hearth. Nearby lay textile remains, a wooden weaving comb, needles and other tools. Cooking and skilled craft work shared this domestic space. Its contents suggest a textile workshop within a house, rather than a modern factory building.

Hundreds of spindle whorls and weights show how important thread and cloth production became at Beycesultan. Finds from the 1700-1500 BCE phases suggest that some household members specialized in weaving. Researchers place larger looms mainly in roomy courtyards and note that tools could be gathered into living or storage rooms afterward. Work equipment had to fit around the rest of home life.

Many Beycesultan weights look like little crescents, with a hole at each end. Their use has been debated, but excavation groups and practical experiments support their role in keeping loom threads under tension. The study discusses how two holes could help separate threads and reduce tangles. Ancient cloth-making involved careful equipment choices, not simply pulling wool until a shirt appeared.

An ivory box recovered at Acemhöyük in 1976 lay in the ashes of a burnt level III building. Its carved scenes include animals and people carrying offerings, while gold, bronze, iron and lapis lazuli decorated its surfaces. The excavator dated it no later than the eighteenth century BCE and suggested connections with northern Syria. The craftsmanship illustrates links between elite patrons and specialized makers.

A stone mould from Acemhöyük shows a seated musician with a five-stringed lyre. Its maker apparently started at the bottom and ran out of room for the head and upper instrument, according to the excavator. The unfinished mould eventually became a wedge in a wall. Even skilled workshops produced mistakes, and a failed project could still find a useful second job.

A tiny eighteenth-century BCE furniture piece, probably from Acemhöyük, was carved from hippopotamus ivory as a seated monkey. Its knees tuck toward its chest and its open mouth reveals teeth. The museum identifies Egyptian-inspired imagery transformed by Anatolian makers. This is evidence of decorative taste and distant connections, not proof that pet monkeys roamed every local home.

Contemporary Kanesh lies outside this map outline, but its excavated neighborhoods provide a useful comparison. Mud-brick houses stood on stone foundations beside paved streets with underground drainage channels. Homes ranged from two rooms to larger complexes, often with an upper storey. The drains show organized urban water management; they do not establish that every Anatolian house had a toilet.

Kanesh’s Assyrian merchants and local Anatolian residents worked together and sometimes married and raised children together. A surviving letter, probably from the city, shows Puzur-Ashur worrying about travel companions reportedly detained on their journey. Business correspondence could carry family anxiety as well as prices and debts. These were particular people in a trading community, not representatives of one uniform Anatolian ethnicity.

How did people learn to write? Studying the Assur-Kanesh correspondence, researcher Cécile Michel distinguishes professional scribal hands from skills taught within families and writing learned through practical work. Some letters are less orderly than others. This neighboring evidence suggests different routes into literacy, without establishing that all children attended schools or that Beycesultan followed the same teaching system.

A contemporary written voice comes from neighboring Kanesh, not from an imagined shared tribal language. Tablet Kt 94/k 1150, dated about 1920-1850 BCE, opens a-na En-um-A-šur qí-bi-ma: “Say to Ennum-Aššur.” This is the published scholarly transliteration of Old Assyrian Akkadian in cuneiform, shown in modern Latin type. Researchers used X-ray tomography to read the tablet inside its clay envelope.

ending.text: The atlas stops this label at 1500 BCE, but it does not record the fall of a single Anatolian state. Beycesultan continued into later Bronze Age phases, with changing buildings and activities. Individual centers followed different histories. The Hittite kingdom and later Anatolian polities need their own accounts; the disappearance of this broad map label is not the disappearance of the region’s inhabitants.
